paragraphs.context: I think it is the central fantasy of childhood
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says every child dreams of being the only one who sees how good someone truly is: because Opal loves Winn-Dixie, everyone can see he is a special dog, and because Winn-Dixie loves Opal, everyone can see she is a special girl. That is the magic of love.
paragraphs.simple: I think the biggest dream of childhood, and maybe of all of life, is this: you alone can see that a person is good and full of promise, even when nobody else can see it. Opal loves Winn-Dixie, so now it is clear to everyone that he is a wonderful dog. And Winn-Dixie is loyal to Opal, so people understand that Opal must be a wonderful child. Love changes how everyone sees them. That is the magic that love works.

paragraphs.context: That summer I found Winn-Dixie was also the summer
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal explains that the summer she found Winn-Dixie was also the summer she and her father moved to Naomi, Florida. She calls her father “the preacher” because church work fills his whole life, and her first name, India, comes from his time as a missionary in that country.
paragraphs.simple: The summer I found Winn-Dixie was the same summer my father and I moved to Naomi, Florida, so he could become the new preacher at the Open Arms Baptist Church. My father is a good man and a good preacher, but it is hard for me to think of him as my daddy, because he spends all his time preaching, thinking about preaching, or getting ready to preach. So in my mind I call him “the preacher.” Before I was born, he worked as a missionary in the country of India, and that is how I got my first name, India. But he calls me by my middle name, Opal, because that was his mother’s name, and he loved her very much.

paragraphs.context: Sometimes he reminded me of a turtle hiding inside its shell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal compares her father to a turtle hiding in its shell: he keeps his thoughts and feelings inside himself and never shows them to the world. Then she asks if the stray dog, a “Less Fortunate,” can stay with them.
paragraphs.simple: I looked hard at my father. Sometimes he made me think of a turtle hiding inside its shell, staying in there with its thoughts and never putting its head out into the world. “Daddy,” I asked, “I was wondering. Could this Less Fortunate dog stay with us for a while?”

paragraphs.context: she hated being a preacher’s wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal’s mother hated being a preacher’s wife because the church women judged everything about her — her clothes, her cooking, her singing — until she felt like a bug under a microscope, watched closely from every side.
paragraphs.simple: Number eight was that my mama hated being a preacher’s wife. She said she just could not stand it when the women at church judged what she was wearing, what she was cooking, and how she was singing. She said it made her feel like a tiny bug under a microscope, with everyone looking closely at her every move.

paragraphs.context: The other thing about the Open Arms that is different
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Open Arms church has no pews; people bring their own folding and lawn chairs, so it sometimes looks more like a parade or a barbecue than a church. Opal thinks the strange little church will suit Winn-Dixie perfectly.
paragraphs.simple: Another thing that makes the Open Arms different from other churches is that it has no long church benches. People bring their own folding chairs and lawn chairs, so sometimes the people sitting there look more like they are watching a parade or sitting at an outdoor barbecue than sitting in church. It is a strange kind of church, and I thought Winn-Dixie would belong there just fine.

paragraphs.context: And then I talked to God about how I was lonely
paragraphs.mainIdea: In her prayer, Opal tells God she is lonely in Naomi because she hardly knows any children, and the few church children do not want to be her friends — they think she would report their bad behavior to her preacher father.
paragraphs.simple: Then I talked to God about being lonely in Naomi, because I did not know many children there, only the ones from church. There were not many children at the Open Arms: just Dunlap and Stevie Dewberry, two brothers who were not twins but looked like twins; and Amanda Wilkinson, whose face always looked tight and unhappy, as if she smelled something bad; and Sweetie Pie Thomas, who was only five and still almost a baby. None of them wanted to be my friend anyway, because they probably thought I would tell the preacher about every little wrong thing they did. Then they would get in trouble with God and with their parents. So I told God I felt lonely, even though I had Winn-Dixie.

paragraphs.context: she didn’t think he was a dog. She thought he was a bear.
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Miss Franny first sees Winn-Dixie standing on his hind legs at the window, she mistakes him for a bear. Opal explains that Winn-Dixie only wants to watch her while she chooses books.
paragraphs.simple: It all started because Winn-Dixie did not like it when I went into the library, since he could not come inside with me. But I showed him how he could stand up on his back legs and look through the window to see me inside choosing my books, and that made him feel okay, as long as he could see me. But the first time Miss Franny Block saw Winn-Dixie standing up that way and looking in the window, she did not think he was a dog at all. She thought he was a bear.

paragraphs.context: mistaking a dog for a bear, but that she had a bad experience
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Franny feels embarrassed about her mistake, but explains that a bear once came into the library long ago and she never fully recovered from the fright. That is why she panicked.
paragraphs.simple: After I pulled her up, she felt shy and embarrassed. She said I must think she was a silly old woman for mistaking a dog for a bear. But she told me that long ago a real bear had come into the Herman W. Block Memorial Library, and it had been a very bad and scary experience for her. She had never quite gotten over it, and that was why she had been so frightened.

paragraphs.context: I imagine I'm the only one left from those days.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Franny finishes her bear story: the bear never came back, and the men in town used to tease her that the bear was still out in the woods reading the book. Then she turns sad, saying she is the only person left from those days because all her old friends are gone.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Franny said she never saw the bear again. But the men in town used to tease her about it, pretending they had seen her bear out in the woods, reading the library book and asking to keep it for one more week. Yes, they really did tease her like that. Then she sighed. She imagined she was the only one left from those old days, the only one who even remembered the bear. All her friends, and everyone she had known when she was young, were all dead and gone.

paragraphs.context: Why don't you go on and tell me everything about yourself,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gloria Dump says her eyes are so bad that she can only see the shape of things, so she must 'see' people with her heart. She asks Opal to tell her everything about herself so she can see Opal with her heart.
paragraphs.simple: Then Gloria Dump made a peanut-butter sandwich for herself and put her false teeth in so she could eat it. When she was done, she told Opal that her eyes were not good at all. She could not see anything but the general shape of things, so she had to depend on her heart to really see people. She asked Opal to go ahead and tell her everything about herself, so that she could see Opal with her heart.

paragraphs.context: I told her how me and the preacher had just moved to Naomi
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal tells Gloria Dump her whole story: the move to Naomi, her mama leaving, the ten things she knows about her mama, the preacher being like a turtle, finding Winn-Dixie, and the new friends and job she got because of him.
paragraphs.simple: Opal told Gloria Dump everything. She told her how she and the preacher had just moved to Naomi and how she had had to leave all her friends behind. She told her about her mama leaving, and she listed out the ten things that she knew about her. She explained that here, in Naomi, she missed her mama more than she ever had back in Watley. She told her about the preacher being like a turtle, always hiding inside his shell. She told her about finding Winn-Dixie in the produce department, and how, because of him, she had become friends with Miss Franny Block, gotten a job working for Otis at Gertrude's Pets, and been invited to Sweetie Pie Thomas's birthday party. She even told Gloria Dump how Dunlap and Stevie Dewberry called her a witch. But she told her they were stupid, mean, bald-headed boys, and she did not believe them — not for long, anyway.

paragraphs.context: it's a fear that goes way beyond normal fears.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The preacher describes the kind of fear Winn-Dixie has: a fear that goes far beyond normal fears and that nobody can talk you out of or reason you out of.
paragraphs.simple: The preacher raised his hand and rubbed his nose. After a minute, he said that this kind of fear goes way beyond normal fears. It is a fear that you cannot be talked out of or reasoned out of.

paragraphs.context: I said, "Play some more music, Otis."
paragraphs.mainIdea: While catching the loose animals, Opal realizes that Otis's guitar music makes them all sit still, like a snake charmer's music. So she shouts for Otis to play more music.
paragraphs.simple: For what felt like a long time, Opal and Otis ran around trying to catch the mice and gerbils and hamsters and snakes and lizards. They kept bumping into each other and tripping over the animals, and Gertrude kept screaming, 'Dog! Dog!' Every time Opal caught something, she put it back in the first cage she saw; she did not care if it was the right cage or not. She just put it in and slammed the door. And the whole time she was chasing things, she was thinking that Otis must be some kind of snake charmer, the way he could play his guitar and make all the animals sit like stones. And then she thought, 'This is silly.' Over the barking and the screaming, she shouted, 'Play some more music, Otis.'

paragraphs.context: I felt like a soldier who had been fighting a hard battle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The daily yelling fights with Dunlap and Stevie Dewberry wear Opal out, so by the time she reaches Gloria's yard she feels like a tired soldier. Gloria's sandwich and coffee bring her back to life.
paragraphs.simple: Opal swore that yelling at Dunlap and Stevie Dewberry every day about wore her out. By the time she got to Gloria Dump's yard, she felt like a soldier who had been fighting a hard battle. Gloria would make her a peanut-butter sandwich straight off, and then she would pour her a cup of coffee with half coffee and half milk, and that would refresh her.

paragraphs.context: I wondered if my mama, wherever she was, had a tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal looks at Gloria's bottle tree and wonders if her mother has a tree like it. She also wonders if she herself is a ghost to her mother, the way her mother sometimes feels like a ghost to her.
paragraphs.simple: Opal stayed where she was and looked at the tree for a long time. She thought about her own mother, who was far away. She wondered whether her mother, wherever she was, also had a tree full of bottles. Then she had a sadder thought: maybe she, Opal, was a ghost to her mother — someone far away and hard to remember — just as her mother sometimes felt like a ghost to her.

paragraphs.context: I held on to him and comforted him and whispered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal holds and comforts Winn-Dixie during thunderstorms, the same kind of comfort he gives to Miss Franny during her fits. But she holds him for a second reason too: so he cannot run away.
paragraphs.simple: When Miss Franny had one of her small fits, it reminded Opal of how Winn-Dixie acted in a thunderstorm. There were many thunderstorms that summer, and Opal had learned to hold Winn-Dixie close when they came. She held him, comforted him, whispered to him, and rocked him — the same kind of comfort Winn-Dixie gave to Miss Franny when she shook. But Opal held him for one more reason too: she held him tight so that he would not run away from home.

paragraphs.context: It’s been a tradition in my family to read the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reading David Copperfield aloud is a family tradition. Miss Franny's great-grandfather Littmus read it to her grandfather every year, and Miss Franny read it to her father when he was old.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Franny explained that David Copperfield was a book, not a person, and that it was about a boy growing up. In her family, people had always read this book out loud to each other. Her great-grandfather, Littmus, read it out loud to her grandfather every single year. Later, when Miss Franny's father was an old man, Miss Franny read the book out loud to him.

paragraphs.context: the only thing that made Littmus forget that he was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Franny describes how terrible the war was for Littmus: always hungry, covered with biting bugs, freezing in winter and suffering in the summer heat. The only time he forgot his misery was when someone was shooting at him — and he was still just a boy.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Franny told the girls they could not imagine the war. Littmus was hungry all the time. His body was covered with tiny biting bugs like fleas and lice. In winter he was so cold he thought he would freeze to death. In summer, nothing was worse than war in the hot weather; it smelled terrible. The strange and sad truth was this: the only time Littmus forgot about being hungry, itchy, hot, or cold was when people were shooting at him. And people shot at him a lot. And he was only a child.

paragraphs.context: Littmus W. Block figured the world was a sorry affair
paragraphs.mainIdea: After crying for his lost family, Littmus felt a strange wish for something sweet. Right then he decided to spend his life putting something sweet into a world that had too many ugly things.
paragraphs.simple: When Littmus came home from the war and found himself alone, he sat on what used to be his front step and cried like a baby. He cried for his mother, his father, his sisters, and for the boy he used to be. When he finished crying, something strange happened: he suddenly wanted something sweet, a piece of candy, which he had not tasted in years. At that moment he made an important decision. He decided that the world was a sad and bad place with too many ugly things in it, so he would spend his life putting something sweet into it. He stood up and started walking all the way to Florida, and while he walked, he planned how to do it.

paragraphs.context: I lay there and thought how life was like a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lying in bed, Opal realizes that life is like a Littmus Lozenge: the sweet and the sad are mixed together, and it is hard to pull them apart.
paragraphs.simple: Opal could not fall asleep right away. She lay in bed and thought about the Littmus Lozenge. She decided that life was just like that candy: sweet things and sad things were all mixed up together, like the candy's flavors. It was very hard to separate the sweet part from the sad part. This idea felt confusing to her.

paragraphs.context: Thinking about her was the same as the hole you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal sweeps slowly to keep Otis company. Thinking about her mother is like touching the empty hole left after losing a tooth — her mind keeps returning to the empty place where her mother should be.
paragraphs.simple: Opal swept the floor very slowly that day because she wanted to stay with Otis and keep him company; she did not want him to feel lonely. It seemed to her that almost everyone in the world was lonely. She thought about her mother. Thinking about her mother felt like what happens after you lose a tooth: your tongue keeps going back to touch the empty hole, again and again. In the same way, Opal's mind kept going back to the empty place inside her — the place where she felt her mother should be.

paragraphs.context: And then it came to me — the solution for
paragraphs.mainIdea: While reading to Gloria, Opal keeps worrying about lonely Otis, who is not allowed to play his guitar for people. Then she suddenly gets an idea that could heal Otis's aching heart — and everyone's.
paragraphs.simple: Opal opened David Copperfield and began to read to Gloria, but her mind was somewhere else. She kept thinking about Otis and worrying about him, because he was not allowed to play his guitar for people anymore. She wanted to find some people who would listen to his music. Then, all at once, the answer came into her head: she had found a plan that could fix Otis's sad, aching heart — and the aching hearts of everyone else too.

paragraphs.context: It looked so pretty that it made my
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal is moved by how beautiful the decorated yard looks, and her full heart makes her wish her mother could share the party.
paragraphs.simple: The yard did look pretty. It looked so pretty that it made my heart feel strange, full and tight inside my chest. And I wished with all my heart that I knew where my mother was, so she could come to the party too.

paragraphs.context: Amanda Wilkinson came and she had her blond
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amanda arrives looking shy and gentle, and Opal, understanding what it feels like to lose someone, feels warm toward her and is extra nice.
paragraphs.simple: Amanda Wilkinson came to the party. Her blond hair was curled, and she looked shy, not as mean as she usually was. I stood very close to her and introduced her to Gloria Dump. I was surprised to find how glad I was to see her. I wanted to tell her that I knew about Carson, and that I understood what it feels like to lose someone, but I said nothing. I was just extra kind to her.

paragraphs.context: Dear God, thank you for warm summer nights
paragraphs.mainIdea: The preacher says grace, thanking God most of all for friends and for the work of loving each other.
paragraphs.simple: Dear God, thank you for warm summer nights, for candlelight, and for good food. But thank you most of all for friends. We thank you for the wonderful and not-always-easy gifts you give us in each other. And we thank you for the work you place in front of us: to love each other as well as we can, in the same way that you love us. We pray in the name of Christ. Amen.

paragraphs.context: There ain’t no way you can hold on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gloria comforts Opal with these words: you cannot force anything to stay; you can only love what you have while you have it.
paragraphs.simple: Come here, child, Gloria Dump said. She reached for me, pulled me close to her, and whispered in my ear: there is no way you can hold on to something that wants to leave, do you understand? You can only love what you have while you still have it.

paragraphs.context: I memorized it so if I didn’t find
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal memorizes her list about Winn-Dixie to keep part of him, then realizes a list can never show who someone really is.
paragraphs.simple: I kept repeating the list of ten things about Winn-Dixie in my head. I learned it by heart the same way I had learned the list of ten things about my mother. I learned it so that if I never found him, I would still have some part of him to keep. But then I thought of something new: a list of things could never show someone the real Winn-Dixie, just as my list of ten things about my mother could never help me really know her. That thought made me cry even harder.

paragraphs.context: I forgot one thing, one very important thing
paragraphs.mainIdea: The preacher promises they will keep looking, and admits he forgot one important thing Opal's mother left behind.
paragraphs.simple: We’ll keep looking, the preacher said. The two of us will keep looking for him. But do you know what? I just understood something, India Opal. When I told you your mother took everything with her, I forgot one thing — one very important thing that she left behind.

paragraphs.context: That dog of yours was all hid underneath
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gloria tells how Winn-Dixie hid under her bed during the storm, smiling and sneezing each time he heard Otis's guitar.
paragraphs.simple: Your dog was hiding under my bed, squeezed in under there as if the world were about to end. But every time he heard Otis play the guitar, he smiled like a happy fool — he smiled so hard that he sneezed.

paragraphs.context: I felt my heart swell up inside me
paragraphs.mainIdea: As her father hums and Otis plays the guitar and Winn-Dixie rests under Gloria's chair, Opal feels her heart fill with pure happiness.
paragraphs.simple: My father started humming a tune, and Otis began playing the notes on his guitar. Winn-Dixie wagged his tail and lay back down under Gloria’s chair. I looked around the room at all the different faces, and my heart filled up inside me with pure, clean happiness.

paragraphs.context: I know ten things about you, and that’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Opal speaks to her mother as if she were standing right beside her: ten things are not enough, but her heart is full now and her father will tell her more.
paragraphs.simple: Mother, I said, as if she were standing right next to me. I know ten things about you, and that is not enough — not nearly enough. But Daddy is going to tell me more; I know he will, now that he understands you are not coming back. He misses you, and I miss you, but my heart does not feel empty anymore. It is full, all the way to the top. I will still think about you, I promise. But probably not as much as I did this summer.

paragraphs.context: the flavor of the Littmus Lozenge opened in my
paragraphs.mainIdea: As the candy melts sweet and sad in her mouth, everyone begins to sing, and Opal listens carefully to learn the song.
paragraphs.simple: Otis laughed and played a few notes on his guitar, and the taste of the candy opened in my mouth like a flower opening up — sweet and sad at the same time. Then Otis, Gloria, Stevie, Miss Franny, Dunlap, Amanda, Sweetie Pie, and my daddy all started to sing a song. And I listened very carefully, so I could learn it the right way.

paragraphs.context: I found it painful to see Opal and Gloria
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author replaced Gone with the Wind with a different book for Opal and Gloria to share, because she cannot honestly recommend the old one.
paragraphs.simple: When I wrote this story more than twenty years ago, I gave Opal and Gloria Dump a famous Southern book to share: Gone with the Wind. But when I read Because of Winn-Dixie again to prepare this anniversary edition, it hurt me to see Opal and Gloria Dump sitting together, side by side, reading from a book that I cannot honestly and with a clear conscience tell my readers to read. I am thankful for this chance to give Opal and Gloria Dump a different book to share — a book that, while not perfect, does not make either of them seem less human.

paragraphs.context: The Dewberry boys use a derogatory word about
paragraphs.mainIdea: The author kept the boys' insulting words because books let readers learn to see people differently, just as the boys do.
paragraphs.simple: The Dewberry boys use an insulting word about Otis and another insulting word about Gloria Dump. I thought about removing those words, but books are a place where readers get a chance to see things in a new way. The Dewberry boys learn to see Otis and Gloria Dump as they truly are. They change their minds; we, as readers, get to change our minds, too.

sentences.context: I think it is the central fantasy of childhood, and maybe of life
sentences.grammar: The word “it” points forward to the long that-clause at the end, which explains what the fantasy is; read the sentence as “the fantasy is that you alone can see...”.
sentences.simple: I think the biggest dream of childhood, and maybe of all life, is this: you alone can see how good someone is, even when no one else can see it.

sentences.context: Not only are we allowed to change, it’s essential that we do
sentences.grammar: “Not only” at the start of the sentence flips the normal word order to “are we” instead of “we are”; this inversion adds strong emphasis.
sentences.simple: We are not only allowed to change; we must change. Change is necessary.

sentences.context: That summer I found Winn-Dixie was also the summer me and the preacher moved
sentences.grammar: The sentence says X “was also” Y: two different descriptions joined by “was” both point to the same summer.
sentences.simple: The summer I found Winn-Dixie was the same summer my father and I moved to Naomi, Florida.

sentences.context: pulling his old turtle head back into his stupid turtle shell
sentences.grammar: This keeps the turtle comparison going: “turtle head” and “turtle shell” stand for the preacher hiding his thoughts and feelings instead of sharing them.
sentences.simple: I could see that he was closing himself off again, hiding his feelings and refusing to talk, just like a turtle pulling its head back into its shell.

sentences.context: exactly the kind of noise that people in an all adult trailer park
sentences.grammar: “That people in an all adult trailer park do not like to hear” is a relative clause describing “noise”; the main point is “It was exactly the kind of noise.”
sentences.simple: People in an adults-only trailer park do not like to hear that kind of noise.

sentences.context: he wasn’t but two or three words into his sermon when there was
sentences.grammar: “Wasn’t but” is an old-fashioned way of saying “had only”; “two or three words into his sermon” means “having just started his sermon”.
sentences.simple: He had only said two or three words of his sermon when a terrible howl came from outside.

sentences.context: One minute, everything was quiet and serious and the preacher was going
sentences.grammar: “One minute X, and the next minute Y” is a fixed pattern meaning the situation suddenly changed completely from X to Y.
sentences.simple: At one moment everything was quiet and serious, and the very next moment everything changed: Winn-Dixie was racing across the room like a furry bullet, chasing the mouse.

sentences.context: She didn’t weigh hardly anything at all
sentences.grammar: Two negatives (“didn’t” and “hardly”) are used together here for emphasis in speech; together they mean “almost nothing.”
sentences.simple: She weighed almost nothing at all; she was very light.

sentences.context: mosquitoes so big they could fly away with you,
sentences.grammar: Uses the pattern 'so + adjective + that' to show an extreme result: the mosquitoes were so big that they could fly away with a person.
sentences.simple: The mosquitoes were so huge that they could carry you away into the sky.

sentences.context: decide if a little-miss-know-it-all librarian was what he was in the mood to eat
sentences.grammar: A question is hidden inside the sentence: the whole 'if'-clause is the object of 'decide', so the bear is deciding the answer to that question.
sentences.simple: The bear sniffed as if he were thinking about whether this clever librarian was something he wanted to eat.

sentences.context: if we get separated for too long, he starts to howl something terrible
sentences.grammar: A conditional 'if'-clause with a get-passive ('get separated'); 'howl something terrible' means 'howl in a terrible way'.
sentences.simple: If Winn-Dixie and I are apart for too long, he starts to howl in a terrible way.

sentences.context: more afraid of losing Winn-Dixie than I was
sentences.grammar: A comparison with words left out: 'than I was' really means 'than I was afraid of having to deal with a dog-eating witch'.
sentences.simple: I was more afraid of losing Winn-Dixie than I was of facing the dog-eating witch.

sentences.context: like it's all happening by accident, like he doesn't intend
sentences.grammar: Two 'like'-clauses ('like' + a full sentence) show how things seemed, not how they really were — the dog pretended he did not mean to climb up.
sentences.simple: He looked away in a different direction so it would seem that getting on the couch was an accident and not his plan.

sentences.context: so early for my first day of work that the CLOSED sign
sentences.grammar: The pattern 'so + adjective + that + result' links cause and result: they were so early that the door was still closed.
sentences.simple: They arrived so early that the shop still had its CLOSED sign up in the window.

sentences.context: in a notebook that he had marked on the outside,
sentences.grammar: The clause 'that he had marked on the outside' is a relative clause telling which notebook it was; the quoted words are what he wrote on the cover.
sentences.simple: Otis wrote down my working hours in a notebook, and on its outside cover he had written the names of the collar and the leash.

sentences.context: The ghosts of all the things I done wrong.
sentences.grammar: Gloria uses “done” as the simple past instead of “did”; this is Southern dialect speech in the story, not a grammar mistake by the author.
sentences.simple: The ghosts are all the bad things I did in the past.

sentences.context: It was the firing on Fort Sumter that started the
sentences.grammar: An it-cleft sentence: “It was X that ...” puts strong stress on X, the one thing that really matters.
sentences.simple: The firing on Fort Sumter is what started the war.

sentences.context: I wouldn’t be standing in this room telling this story
sentences.grammar: An unreal past conditional: “wouldn’t be ... if he was killed” imagines something that did not happen, in order to prove the opposite is true.
sentences.simple: If Littmus had died in the war, I would not be here now to tell you this story.

sentences.context: something else I didn’t have a name for, something that
sentences.grammar: The word “that” is left out before “I didn’t have a name for”, and “for” is left at the end; English often drops “that” and strands the preposition.
sentences.simple: It tasted like root beer and strawberry, plus one more taste I could not name, and that taste made me feel a little sad.

sentences.context: I liked the way it sounded, like there was music
sentences.grammar: “The way it sounded” means “how it sounded”; here “way” works like “how”, not like “road”.
sentences.simple: I liked how the word sounded; it felt as if music was hiding inside it.

sentences.context: I went right on playing my music
sentences.grammar: "Went right on playing" means "kept on playing without stopping"; "right on" adds strong emphasis that he did not stop at all.
sentences.simple: I kept playing my music all the time they were talking to me.

sentences.context: that the whole world has an aching heart
sentences.grammar: “Sometimes” is placed in the middle, breaking “I believe ... that ...”; the main idea is “I believe that the whole world has an aching heart.”
sentences.simple: I think the whole world feels a deep sadness in its heart.

sentences.context: It looked so pretty that it made my
sentences.grammar: Uses a so + adjective + that result clause, plus a wish clause in the past tense for something the speaker wants but does not have.
sentences.simple: The yard was very pretty. It made my heart feel strange and full. I wished very strongly that I knew where my mother was, so she could come to the party too.

sentences.context: like he was a wild animal that I
sentences.grammar: like he was makes a comparison; that I was trying to get to take is a relative clause, and get someone to do means to cause or persuade them to do it.
sentences.simple: I spoke to him very softly and quietly, as if he were a wild animal and I was trying to make him take food from my hand.

sentences.context: the task you put down before us, of
sentences.grammar: The noun task is followed by a hidden that/which relative clause (the task you put down before us); of loving each other explains what the task is.
sentences.simple: And we thank you for the job you give us: to love each other as well as we can, the way you love us.

sentences.context: There ain’t no way you can hold on
sentences.grammar: A double negative (ain’t no way) in non-standard Southern speech means the opposite of what the words seem to say: there is no way.
sentences.simple: It is not possible to keep something that wants to leave, do you understand?

sentences.context: I memorized it so if I didn’t find
sentences.grammar: so starts a purpose clause with a conditional inside it (if I didn’t find him, I would have), about an imagined future.
sentences.simple: I learned the list by heart so that, if I never found him, I would still have something of him to keep.

sentences.context: there ain’t a song he don’t know
sentences.grammar: A double negative (ain’t ... don’t) in dialect speech means the opposite: there is no song he does not know, so he knows every song.
sentences.simple: He knows every song there is.

sentences.context: squeezed under there like the world was about
sentences.grammar: like makes an exaggerated comparison, and was about to end uses about to for something that feels very near.
sentences.simple: Your dog was hiding under my bed, squeezed in so tight it looked like the world was ending.

sentences.context: He did something I never in a million years
sentences.grammar: Something (that) a Dewberry boy would do is a shortened relative clause; never in a million years is placed in the middle for strong surprise.
sentences.simple: He did something I never, ever thought a Dewberry boy would do.

sentences.context: the flavor of the Littmus Lozenge opened in my
sentences.grammar: A metaphor compares the spreading flavor to a flower blooming; all sweet and sad describes the flavor itself.
sentences.simple: The taste of the candy spread in my mouth like a flower opening, sweet and sad at the same time.

sentences.context: I found it painful to see Opal and Gloria
sentences.grammar: found it painful to see means felt pain when seeing; the long sentence stacks a when-clause and a that-clause in a formal written style.
sentences.simple: But when I read the book again to get ready for this new edition, it hurt me to see Opal and Gloria Dump sitting side by side, reading a book I cannot honestly tell my readers to read.
